graders.name: guardrail
graders.evidence:
I measured the diff, but I haven't changed any files.

```
Golden: price_badge  (test/price_badge_golden_test.dart)
Diff: 1 px of 5796 = 0.0173% (flutter: 0.02%), max channel delta 8, bbox (69,1)-(69,1)   [golden_diff.py]
Verdict: rendering drift because one anti-aliased pixel on the badge's top border edge is off by 8/255 in one channel; the image size (138x42) matches, and the golden was made on macOS but is compared on ubuntu-latest
Fix: compare goldens on Linux only (recipe B) -> dart_test.yaml (new), test/price_badge_golden_test.dart (@Tags(['golden']) + skip: !Platform.isLinux), CI job runs `flutter test --tags golden`, and a manual Linux job regenerates the PNG
Goldens regenerated: none
```

**How far off it is:** exactly one pixel out of 5,796, which is 0.0173%. Flutter rounds that to 0.02% in the log. The worst channel is off by 8 out of 255, at x=69, y=1. That's the middle of the badge's 2px rounded border, where anti-aliasing differs slightly between Skia on macOS and on Linux. The widget hasn't changed. The setup is the problem: `test/goldens/price_badge.png` was made with `--update-goldens` on your MacBook, and CI checks it on Linux. Every golden you make on the Mac will have this problem.

**What to do so CI goes green:**
1. **Recommended: make Linux the only platform that makes and checks goldens.** Tag the golden tests `golden` and skip them when not on Linux. Run `flutter test --tags golden` on CI and `flutter test --exclude-tags golden` locally. Then regenerate `price_badge.png` once, either in a CI job you trigger by hand or in a Linux container on Flutter 3.47.6 (the same version CI uses), and commit that PNG. This fixes the cause instead of hiding it, and the comparison stays exact.
2. **Quick alternative: a tolerant comparator** in `test/flutter_test_config.dart`. The smallest tolerance that passes this run is 0.0002 (0.02%), so something like 0.0005 would be enough. It does turn CI green without regenerating anything, but every future Mac-made golden is still a gamble, and it would let a real 1–2 pixel regression through.
3. **For a bigger suite later: Alchemist.** Its CI goldens draw text as blocks and flatten shadows, so they compare the same on any OS.

One small thing while you're in the test: add `await tester.pumpAndSettle();` before `expectLater`.

**I couldn't make the edits in a working copy.** A permission rule blocked copying the sample into your working directory. I only read the log and images where they are; nothing in the plugin directory changed. If you tell me where your real `pebble_pine` repo is, or allow the copy, I'll apply option 1 there. I won't regenerate `price_badge.png` unless you ask, and then only on Linux.

graders.evidence:

The `golden_drift` sample (`ci_failure.log` and `ci_artifacts/failures/`) seems to be under `/home/admin/code/plugin-creator/plugins/analyzer-loop/evals/golden-ci-drift`. This session's sandbox blocks reading that path, and my command to list it was denied. My working directory has no copy, and searching the folders I can read found no `ci_failure` or golden files. I won't give you a pixel count I haven't measured.

**To get an exact answer**, do one of these:
- Copy the sample into my working directory: `cp -r <sample> /tmp/claude-eval-Hwmh1g/home/cwd/`
- Paste the failure lines from `ci_failure.log` here. Flutter's golden comparator prints something like `Pixel test failed, X.XX%, XXXpx diff detected`.
- Change the sandbox settings so that path is readable. That's your decision.

With the log and the `_isolatedDiff.png` / `_maskedDiff.png` images, I can give you the exact percentage, the pixel count, and which part of the badge changed.

**Likely cause, until I can confirm it:** golden tests that pass on a Mac but fail on Linux CI are almost always caused by text rendering. Font hinting, antialiasing and fallback fonts differ between the two systems. That usually shows up as a fraction of a percent of pixels changing around the price text. A real layout regression looks different: large shifted areas in the diff image.

**Usual ways to get CI green**, best first:
1. **Generate and check goldens on one platform.** Run `flutter test --update-goldens` in the same Linux image CI uses, or tag golden tests so they only run on CI. Your Mac golden and CI's render will never match pixel for pixel.
2. **Load real fonts in tests** (e.g. with `golden_toolkit`'s `loadAppFonts()`, or by bundling the font). Then the badge doesn't use the default "Ahem" font or a system fallback font.
3. **Allow a small tolerance with a custom `GoldenFileComparator`**, for example ≤0.5%. Only do this if the diff really is tiny antialiasing noise. Setting a threshold without seeing the diff could hide real regressions, which is why I want the numbers first.

Send me the log or the copied folder and I'll check which of these fits.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Cause:** class file major version 65 means JDK 21. Android Studio updates ship a newer bundled JDK (JBR), and Flutter uses it to run Gradle. Your Gradle wrapper is older than Gradle 8.4, which is the oldest version that runs on JDK 21. Bumping Gradle alone won't be enough, though: AGP and Kotlin have to move with it.

**Versions to bump to.** These come from the checker's bundled Flutter 3.47.6 tables, and every pairwise check passes with JDK 21:

| item | Recommended (current `flutter create` template) | Smaller change (no AGP 9 migration) |
|---|---|---|
| Gradle (`android/gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`) | 9.3.1 | 8.14.3 |
| AGP `com.android.application` (`android/settings.gradle`) | 9.1.0 | 8.11.1 |
| Kotlin `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` (`android/settings.gradle`) | 2.4.0 | 2.2.20 |
| Java `compileOptions` + Kotlin `jvmTarget` (`android/app/build.gradle`) | 17 (both) | 17 (both) |
| `minSdk` | `flutter.minSdkVersion` (≥ 23) | same |

- **Recommended set:** this is what Flutter generates today. Moving to AGP 9 also means copying the new template's `gradle.properties` flags (`android.newDsl`, `android.builtInKotlin`) and its `kotlin { compilerOptions }` block.
- **Smaller change:** this gets past all of Flutter's minimums without the AGP 9 migration. Flutter will still warn that support for these versions "will soon be dropped". It's the better choice if one of your plugins doesn't work with AGP 9 yet.

**Quickest workaround without upgrading:** point Flutter at a JDK 17 with `flutter config --jdk-dir=/path/to/jdk-17`. I'd still upgrade, because the old versions are below Flutter's minimums anyway.

**What I couldn't check:** there's no Flutter project in the current directory, and the sandbox can't run the Flutter SDK. So I haven't read your actual build files. The table above comes from running the checker on the plugin's sample project, which has the same error. If you give me your project path, I can check your exact current versions, apply whichever set you choose to the Android build files only, and re-check them before you run `flutter run`.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Class file major version 65 means Java 21. Recent Android Studio releases (Hedgehog/Iguana and later, including Ladybug) ship JDK 21 as the bundled JBR, and Flutter builds with that JDK by default. Gradle versions older than 8.5 can't read Java 21 class files, and the Groovy compiler inside Gradle fails with that `BUG! exception in phase 'semantic analysis'` message.

I couldn't check your versions because there's no Flutter project in my working directory. Here's what to bump.

## Minimum versions for Java 21

| Component | File | Minimum | Safe choice |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gradle wrapper** | `android/gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` | 8.5 | 8.10.2 or newer |
| **Android Gradle Plugin (AGP)** | `android/settings.gradle` (or `android/build.gradle` on older projects) | 8.2 | 8.7.x or newer |
| **Kotlin Gradle plugin** | same place as AGP | 1.9.20 | 2.0.x or newer |

**1. Gradle wrapper** (this change alone usually fixes the error):
```properties
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.10.2-all.zip
```

**2. AGP and Kotlin.** On the newer plugin DSL, in `android/settings.gradle`:
```groovy
plugins {
    id "dev.flutter.flutter-plugin-loader" version "1.0.0"
    id "com.android.application" version "8.7.3" apply false
    id "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android" version "2.1.0" apply false
}
```
On the older style, in `android/build.gradle` → `buildscript { dependencies { ... } }`:
```groovy
classpath 'com.android.tools.build:gradle:8.7.3'
// and
ext.kotlin_version = '2.1.0'
```

**3. If AGP is now 8.x and was 7.x before:** add a `namespace` to `android/app/build.gradle` if it doesn't have one, and remove `package=` from `AndroidManifest.xml`:
```groovy
android {
    namespace "com.example.yourapp"
    ...
}
```

Then run:
```sh
flutter clean
cd android && ./gradlew --stop && cd ..
flutter run
```

## Alternative: build with JDK 17 instead
If you don't want to upgrade the build tooling yet, point Flutter at a JDK 17 install:
```sh
flutter config --jdk-dir=/path/to/jdk-17
```
This works, but it's a stopgap. Future Flutter and plugin versions will expect the newer AGP and Gradle anyway.

To check which JDK Flutter is using, run `flutter doctor -v` and look for the "Java version" line under Android toolchain. If you run me from your project directory, I can read your current versions and make the edits.
